utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody once again today. May the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Appearances for today, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to the Trial Chamber, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution today, Daryl Mundis, Kyle Wood, and our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson, representing General Rasim Delic. Lana Deljkic is our case manager, and also our legal assistant on the case, Asja Zujo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution, in completing its opening, has just a few remaining topics to deal with, the first being the issue of compensation for members of the Mujahedin Detachment. And I start by quoting from paragraph 139 of the Defence Pre-Trial Brief, which indicated that the Mujahedin never received monthly salaries from the ARBiH. I'm not specifically going to address the issue of monthly salaries, but I will say this: The Prosecution intends to lead evidence during the course of this trial in the form of pay records that clearly indicate that at least at the conclusion of the war, members of the Mujahedin Detachment, including foreign members, were compensated for their service in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I turn now to PT2887. This is one of many documents, similar documents, which are from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of Defence. This first record that you see before you relates to an individual named Halid Ibrahim. And if you look again, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of Defence, we'll see excerpts from this is document. Mr. Ibrahim served in the armed forces from the 13th of September, 1992 until 25 December 1995, and indicates that his compensation was 16.000 Deutsche marks. Similarly, Mohammed el-Saidi served in the same period of time, that is, 13th of September, 1992 until 25 December, 1995, and was similarly compensated 16.000 Deutsche marks for his service in the ARBiH. Following up on that, this same large collection of pay records indicates what are actually a receipt book; and, again, if you look closely on this document, you will see individual names. You'll see, under the column number 5, an abbreviation for demobilised or "Demob." demobilised. Column 12 - and, again, this excerpts from the document - Column 12 indicates the amounts in Deutsche marks that these individuals were paid for their military service; and then we see the signatures of these individuals, which would lead to the conclusion that they actually received the funds in question. And, again, this issue, we would submit, will go to demonstrating clearly that these foreign fighters were, in fact, members of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let me turn to another indicia: Promotion, military promotions for members of the Mujahedin Detachment and its leaders. PT1771 is a document dated 25 July 1994. Keep in mind what I told you yesterday about the knowledge of the leadership of the ARBiH concerning members of the Mujahedin Detachment. We spoke about Operation Vranduk, we spoke about the killing of Paul Goodale, we spoke about the knowledge of the criminality of certain members of that unit. Yet on the 25th of July, 1994, we see a proposal for the promotion of ranks, and this document is addressed to the ARBiH Presidency. And in this document, we see, among the individuals proposed for promotion to the rank of captain first class, Abu Maali, 3rd Corps, El Mujahedin Detachment Commander. Later in this document, with respect to a proposal for the rank of captain, we see a number of additional El Mujahedin Detachment leaders, including Muatez, Abu Aiman, Abu Haris. This document at least bears the typed signature of Rasim Delic. It's a bit unclear, because of the stamp, whether the accused actually signed it, but it's certainly on the letterhead of the Main Staff commander and certainly bears his typed name. Next, let's turn to honours for the Mujahedin Detachment and its leader; again, 1995, December 1st. This is a document that clearly indicates that with regard to the third anniversary of the ARBiH, and owing to exceptional results achieved in carrying out combat and other assignments: "I hereby issue the following order," commending the units listed below. The first unit listed is the Mujahedin Unit. Later in the document, we see commendations for individuals, including Abu Maali. This document is signed by the accused, Rasim Delic. On 23 December 1995, we see a similar document: "Based upon the proposal of the 3rd Corps commander, I hereby award for their overall contribution to the armed resistance, to the aggressor against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially for personal courage demonstrated in combat operations in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, the Golden Lily," which is the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina's highest award. A number of individuals are listed, including obviously some individuals whose names would indicate that they do not come from Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's also interesting, in this respect, that one of these names is of a German individual, and we will lead evidence that some of the Mujahedin came from West European countries as well. This document similarly is signed by the accused Rasim Delic. Let's turn now almost to the final chapter of this opening, to the issue of disbandment of the Mujahedin Detachment. PT2809, dated 12 December 1995, with a handwritten notation in the middle. And, again, we have the Bosnian version at the top and the English translation; in the middle of the Bosnian translation, a handwritten note: "Personally delivered to General Mahmuljin," again at that point in time the 3rd Corps commander. This document relates to the disbandment of the Mujahedin Detachment. Under paragraph 1: "Disband the current El Mujahedin Unit of the ARBiH, 3rd Corps." Subparagraph (c): "Foreign citizens, volunteers, former members of the war unit, together with their personal equipment, are to be dismissed from the unit not later than 31 December 1995, with the provision of their compulsory departure from the country no later than 10 January 1996." Subparagraph (f): "All material and technical equipment owned by the ARBiH are to be redistributed to other units of the 3rd Corps." And under paragraph 2, "Final Provisions," again, a repetition of the requirement that this order, the disbandment and departure from the territory of Bosnia, is to be completed by 10 January 1996, along with a requirement that stamps, seals, and documentation that are unnecessary to be kept are to be inventoried and burned in the presence of a committee. Again, the disbandment order signed, we would submit, by the accused Rasim Delic. This order, these documents that you've just seen, were a requirement of Article 3 of Annex 1 of the Dayton Agreement ending the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, by which all foreign fighters were required to leave the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We will lead evidence that prior to the disbandment of the Mujahedin Detachment, the accused, along with President Izetbegovic, the President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, met with the leadership of the Mujahedin Detachment and informed them that the unit would be officially disbanded. Yesterday, Your Honours, I told you that this case was about values, decisions, and inaction. You've heard a brief sketch of where the Prosecution expects the evidence to lead. I've also indicated that, in many respects, inaction speaks louder than words. In closing this opening, the Prosecution points to one instance where the actions of the accused are consistent with his inaction. After the official disbandment of the Mujahedin Detachment, the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held a farewell function in honour of the Mujahedin Detachment. The accused, Rasim Delic, attended that farewell ceremony. Your Honours, the Prosecution is prepared to proceed in the case against General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Madam Vidovic, at the pre-trial conference, the other day, the Defence indicated that it is not the intention of the Defence to make opening statements or to make statements by the accused at this stage. Do you confirm that that's still the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is still the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis, call your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Andrew Hogg, and my colleague, Mr. Wood, will be leading this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. While we are waiting for the witness to come and take the stand, the Registrar will take a few moments to assign exhibit numbers to those 50 or so documents that the Trial Chamber indicated must be given exhibit numbers individually.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On the 15th of June, 2007, the Trial Chamber issued a decision to admit the 48 so-called Law Library documents; and, subsequently, yesterday, there was a clarification to that particular order; whereby, the index prefacing those 48 documents were also -- was also admitted. And there was an oral order to assign exhibit numbers to the index as well as the 48 documents. Following that particular written decision, as well as the oral order, the index will be admitted as Exhibit number 1, and the 48 documents consisting of the Law library will be assigned Exhibit numbers 2 to 49. Secondly, on the 9th of July, the Trial Chamber issued an order to admit statements -- further statements, transcripts, and exhibits of (redacted) and to assign one exhibit number. Pursuant to that order, all collection referred to earlier will be Exhibit number 50. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon, Mr. Hogg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, please, stand up and take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hogg.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What's your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I'm the head of press for the British Charity, the medical foundation for the care of victims of torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did you do before that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I was a journalist for 25 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What was your beat in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: In 1992, I was the Middle East correspondent for "The Sunday Times" of London.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did that exactly entail?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It entailed covering a very wide beat, in fact, that stretched essentially from Morocco to Afghanistan. In the middle of 1992, it expanded to include the conflict in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I've been asked to slow down a little bit. Since we both speak English, we have a tendency to answer each other very quickly, but the interpreters need time to catch up. I apologise for that, and I'll do my best to slow down.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mentioned that in 1992, your beat expanded into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court why that is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Well, to two reasons, really. The Israeli-Palestine conflict went into abeyance because there were meetings that nobody knew about taking place in a farmhouse outside Oslo, so things were relatively quiet on that front. I was also -- having travelled extensively in Muslim countries in the months preceding my first trip to Bosnia, I was also aware of the fact that the fate of the Muslims of Bosnia was of considerable interest to people in most of the countries I was covering at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So if your beat expanded into Bosnia and Herzegovina, what did that mean for you on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Well, between 1992 and 1994, I made, I think, in total some seven trips to Croatia and Bosnia. I spent almost a year in total covering the conflict there. I would typically go in for about six weeks and then either return to London or go on to some other country to continue working; and then I would return to Bosnia, I would say, sort of a month or two later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now some questions about your first trip to Bosnia. Can you tell the Court when that was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: The first trip to Bosnia, from memory, I flew out to Croatia at the end of July in 1992, and I was there for approximately a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And during the course of that month --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm sorry, Mr. Hogg. The question was to Bosnia, not to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I should clarify that. I flew out to Croatia, where I spent a week or two weeks, and then I went on from there to Bosnia, where I stayed until the end of August. August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, that was my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, In the year preceding your first trip to Bosnia, what countries had you been in?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I have been in Algeria, I have been to Afghanistan, I have been to Kurdistan, and I have been -- I think, by that time, I would certainly have been in Israel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, during this first trip, were you travelling with anybody?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: My first trip, I met up with a "Sunday Times" photographer at -- in Zagreb, in Croatia, and we travelled, together with a Croatian interpreter, down into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What's the name of the photographer?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: His name is Simon Townsley.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recall exactly when you went to Bosnia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I can't put a precise date on it. But, I think, as I was there for a month, I would assume it would have been the start of week three.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how did you get to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We took a -- we took a car ferry from Rijeka down to Split, and we then hired a car in Split and we travelled over-land into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you have any story in particular in mind when you arrived in Bosnia in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had one in Split. I had been making inquiries, really sort of about the situation generally of a group of young men who were acting as the sort of press liaison officers for the Croat leader of Herzegovina. And I asked - and I can't remember why I would have asked this question - but I asked if they knew the whereabouts of the Mujahedin. I was curious as to whether foreign Mujahedin had arrived in Bosnia, because I had firsthand experience, both in Algeria and in Afghanistan itself, of the -- of the influence of these fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So when you travelled to Bosnia, what was your destination?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Well, from Split, asking one of these young men the whereabouts of the Mujahedin, he told me that I should go to Travnik if I wanted to find foreign fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So did you proceed to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did you do? What's the first thing you did when you got there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: The first thing I did when we reached Travnik was go to the local army headquarters, Bosnian Army headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how did you know where to find the local Bosnian Army headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I can't be totally precise, but I have absolutely no doubt we would have been told where to find it by one of the check-points that we would have had to have navigated on our way into Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what made you certain that it was a military headquarters for the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: There were men in uniforms, men and women in military uniforms, and there was clearly a communication centre of some kind in one of the rooms. It was quite evidently the headquarters of a fighting force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, may I ask you to remember - you are used to it - to remember to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, Mr. Hogg, why is it that you chose to go to the military headquarters as the first order of business on your arrival?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Essentially, to get permission to travel and to work in the area. That particular conflict was characterised by what I took to be sort of a hangover, in a sense, from the days of communism, which was that everybody seemed to require some kind of permission. Everybody asked to see some kind of document giving one permission to be wherever one was, so it was common sense that you equipped yourself with as many bits of paper as possible from as many different authorities as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court where in Travnik you found this military headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It was in a building which I took to have been, in happier times, a restaurant complex. It was by a waterfall in a fairly senior part of the town. I assumed that prior to the conflict, tourist would have eaten there, and perhaps they -- I'm not sure if there was accommodation or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When you got to the military headquarters, did you make contact with anybody?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We met, at the headquarters, a woman officer in the Bosnian Army. She was, in a sense, introduced to us as what one took to be their version of a press liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how was this woman dressed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: She was in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you ask her?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Well, I think we would have asked for an overview of the -- of the situation at that time. The Serbs were just outside the town. Parts of the town were under bombardment. But during the course of conversation, I also asked about the whereabouts of the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how did she respond to that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: In twofold, really. She told us that the foreign fighters were living in a couple of houses next to the wooden mosque in the centre of Travnik, a well-known historic mosque; but she also told us that they occasionally visited the centre. And we asked, therefore, whether she could make representations to them, to see whether they would give us an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how did she respond to that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: She agreed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What did you do with the information about the fact that some Mujahedin were living in a particular area in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We went and banged on the door. There was no answer. I have every reason to believe that we would have spoken to anybody in the neighbourhood. We would have banged on other doors as well, to see if anybody would throw any light on the presence of these people, and I think that we were actually told that they hadn't been seen for a couple of days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Well, events intervened, inasmuch as there was a peace conference starting in London; and to mark that fact, the Serb Air Force bombed a factory in Novi Travnik, which is sort of the newly-built township next to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you proceed to that area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We were, for some reason, at the hospital when cars began arriving with casualties, and so we went as rapidly as we could to the site of the air raid. And it was there that we -- we spoke to a group of Croatian police officers, and there may have been Croatian military as well. And during the course of the conversation - we were there for some time - they wanted us to inspect the damage. They wanted us to -- to look at something that they claimed had been napalm. I wasn't convinced it was napalm, but it was some kind of incendiary substance. But during the latter part of the conversation, I then switched it to, "What about foreign fighters?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did they tell you about foreign fighters?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I, from memory, think -- I am certain that they directed us towards Zenica; but by the same token - I can't remember if it was that day or the previous day - we also went to a little village called Turbe, which is on the front line between the Serbian forces and, what was at that stage, both the Croat and Bosnian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Why did you go to Turbe?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Specifically, to look for the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just get clarity. You said you were directed to Turbe by the Croatian military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said the point is that the Croatian police and military, I think, when I asked them about the Mujahedin, suggested that I went to look in a town called Zenica. And what I said is I'm not clear whether it was after that or before that that we also went to look in a village called Turbe for the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'll ask you about -- I'll ask you about those places.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: First of all, Turbe. You said you went to Turbe. Did you make contact with anybody there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes. We arrived at -- there was intense mortar bombardment taking place, and you couldn't remain in the open without considerable risk. So we went into a building, and we met there two or three Bosnian military personnel. And the thing that stuck in my mind was, in another part of the building, there were Croat military personnel. And it was quite clear that there was pretty scant communication between the two sides, even though they were both on the same side against the Serbs at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you inquire there about the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what were you told?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Well, it's a long time ago. Basically, we were told that, yes, there were Mujahedin fighting on the front line, but I'm pretty sure that we were told that they weren't on that particular part of the front line at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mentioned also that at some point you went to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recall if that was before or after?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That would have been after. That would have been after the trip to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when you got to Zenica, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: When we went to Zenica, we went to talk to Croats because we thought that we would probably get more information from members of the Croatian military.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Well, because we worked on the assumption that they wouldn't have been too happy about the presence of Mujahedin; whereas, we suspected that had we gone to the Bosnian military, that we might have sort of been stonewalled, effectively. When I say "the Croat military," it was, in fact, Croat police officers that we met. Now, whether there were Croat soldiers there or not, I can't be sure. But it was certainly the information that I was seeking, I was given by Croatian police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what information was that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: They confirmed that the Mujahedin were in town. They expressed a great deal of disquiet about their appearance. They said that these fighters were characterised by the new communications equipment they had and vehicles, four-by-fours, that they had. And they said that if we wanted to find them, we should visit an old people's home, which was apparently their base.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you proceed to that retirement home?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did you find there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I found a group of Bosnian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, when you say "Bosnian soldiers," were they local or were they foreign?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: These were local. These were Bosnian soldiers. When you say "were they local," I was -- one or two of them seemed to be a cut above the sort of ordinary militiaman. One of them, in particular, was clearly very well educated, spoke very good English, and told me that they were there effectively to look after the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how were these people attired?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: They were in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you see any foreign Mujahedin during your visit to this retirement home?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No. We were told that they were out on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were you told how many Mujahedin were staying there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I don't recall. I would -- I know it's a question I would have asked. It would have been apparent to me that there wouldn't have been huge numbers, but I can't recall the precise information I was given. But certainly, I was given to understand that there were -- you know, that there was a body of men there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you told that there were Mujahedin staying there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: At any time during this trip around Turbe, Zenica, did you ever have occasion to stop back in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: The only time I had occasion to go back to Travnik was once I had found the Mujahedin, and they said that I needed permission from the military before they would speak to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, following your trip to Zenica and your visit to the retirement home, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We -- we were given to understand that we might find the Mujahedin. The guys in the retirement home, from memory, weren't too clear themselves precisely where the Mujahedin were, on which bit of the front line. We took ourselves off to the south to a town called Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could interrupt just for a moment, one other thing about Zenica. You said that they weren't that clear about where they were. Did they give you any indication about how you could find out more information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: They gave me a telephone number of a senior officer --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: -- and suggested that I call him. And I, certainly, did try to call that number and didn't find the gentleman I should have been speaking to, which I suspect is why we then took ourselves off to visit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, a senior officer in which military?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It would be the Bosnian military.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. So I interrupted you. You said that after Zenica, you went to Visoko?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We went to Visoko, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And where did you go when you got to Visoko?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Visoko was under bombardment at the time, and you couldn't go wandering around. We parked the car and got out and then became aware of a group of women at the side of the road -- at the side of the road, gesturing very frantically to us to get down. We had apparently parked in Sniper Alley. We went -- we dived across the road and realised that we were outside a hospital, and so went into the hospital to make inquiries there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did you find out when you went into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I met a very stressed-out woman doctor down in the basement, which was full of casualties, and I asked her about the Mujahedin. And through my interpreter, she gave me to understand that a force of 100-plus had been through very recently. I didn't actually believe her. I thought that the number sounded to me very unlikely. She was very distracted, and she was in the middle of a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: About an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And where did you proceed after you left Visoko?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We went back up to Zenica. We were en route, I think, to Travnik when we stopped at a roadblock and, once again, asked where were the Mujahedin and were directed to the village of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recall who it was that was maintaining this check-point?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It was kind of, you know, getting late in the afternoon. It was a raggle-taggle army. I think it was local Bosnia militia, but I couldn't be certain. Certainly, it was locals. It wasn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: At this point, you had contact with the HVO, the Bosnian Croats. Were the people who were maintaining this check-point, were they Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No, I don't think they were. I think they were Bosnian. I think even to call them Bosnian Army would be to sort of elevate their status. They were -- they were local men in a sort of -- from memory, a sort of variety of bits of uniform. Yeah, from memory, they were people who were simply, I guess, sort of trying to save their neighbourhood. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So up to this point, had you had occasion to see any Mujahedin throughout your trip?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So at the check-point, they told you to go to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What did you do then with that information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We drove as fast as we could to Mehurici. The reality was it was getting late in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to get from the check-point to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Not that long. It would have been about half an hour max, I should think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when you got to Mehurici, how did you go about confirming this information that you had?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: On entering the village, there was a woman or a couple of women walking on the opposite side of the road. The interpreter wound down the window and asked them where the Arabs were, and they pointed further up the road, saying that they had passed by only a couple of minutes earlier. And so we went off in hot pursuit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And did you come to see those Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We rounded a corner and there were two four-by-fours parked, and there were a group of men, armed, standing around. As we drove up, my memory is that they looked rather surprised to see us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how many men were standing in the group?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would -- I would have thought between -- somewhere around a dozen. That's what my memory tells me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And under those conditions, could you make any assessment about the makeup, the composition of that group?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I made a very rapid assessment. I recognised that there were at least two men there who I took to be from the Bosnian Army. They were in military uniform. The others I instantly regarded as Mujahedin. In Afghanistan, I had had the misfortune to come across the Arab Mujahedin there, and this was -- you know, this was a reenactment of that, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And could you determine what, precisely, they were doing in the group?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No. I think from memory, I think they were washing their jeeps, but I can't be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And could you describe the jeeps?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. They were newish-looking. They weren't military.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So at this point what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I got out and I walked towards them, and in my best BBC voice I said, "Does anybody here speak English?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what do you mean by your best BBC voice?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to sound authoritative and I wanted to sound very plausible, and I wanted to convey the impression of being a thoroughly professional journalist, which in those sort of circumstances is basically your one defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you receive any response to your question, "Does anybody here speak English?"

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Well, much to my surprise, a gentleman that I later learned to be Abdel Aziz, stepped forward and said, "Yes, I do. Who are you and what do you want?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how did you come to know that this person was Abdel Aziz?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: He told me that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you describe him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: He was dressed in military-style garb. It wasn't a uniform, as such. There was certainly camouflage. I think it was a camouflaged jacket and trousers. His hair was red, and from my experience in Afghanistan I took that to mean that he had henna'ed his hair and his beard in preparation for death.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could I have the Exhibit P06157, page 4, shown to the witness. For the record, it's page 4 of the exhibit that I need. The ERN number, if that will help, is 0471-7266. For the record, I see that -- I guess I should ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you see a photograph on the screen before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And do you recognise the person depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's Abdel Aziz.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: This is the person you spoke with on that day?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So did you have a conversation with Mr. Aziz?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I asked him if he would give me an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did he say?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: He said that provided I got permission from the Bosnian Army, that he would grant me that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What did you do with this information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It was quite clear that there was no point pressing him. The thing that we needed with utmost urgency was to get the necessary permission. I established with him that if we went to Travnik, to the military command, and got that permission, that he wouldn't have disappeared by the time we got back. As I said, it was late in the day. There was no way that we were going to get back there that night. And so I established with him that if I returned early the following morning with the relevant permission, that he would be there, able to give me an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: After he assured you of that, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We went immediately to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And where in Travnik did you go?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We went to the military command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did you do when you got to the military command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I sent the interpreter in to get the necessary permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how long was she inside?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: About ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what happened after she came back out?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: She came out waving a piece of paper, and we were absolutely elated, and we then drove back to Kiseljak, which is where we had been staying because that was the one place in Central Bosnia that we had communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, this piece of paper, did you examine it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I would have, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what can you tell me about it --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: -- or tell the Court about it? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It was an official-looking document, but I couldn't read what it actually said precisely because I didn't speak the language. But I was satisfied that it looked sufficient to put Mr. Aziz's mind at rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What language was it written in, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It was written in the local language, which in those days -- I suppose you could call it Bosnian there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And were there any other markings on the permission?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: There would have been a stamp, because that would have given it authenticity. There was probably a signature, but it's a long time ago and I can't remember absolutely precisely what was there and what wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So how long were you in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We spent the night in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what time did you leave in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Very early. I think we left at about 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We went straight back to Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please make pauses between questions and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When you got to Mehurici, where did you go within the town?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We knew, because I think that that's where we had last seen Mr. Aziz, that he was based in what we took to be a school. So we went immediately -- on the main road, we went immediately to that school, and I spoke to somebody outside who, from memory, was clearly on guard duty of some kind, and asked that person to tell Mr. Aziz that we had got the necessary permission and, yeah, we were at his -- waiting at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And did Mr. Aziz appear?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. He didn't appear immediately. There was a coffee bar opposite, and we -- because we were attracting considerable attention at that time, we decided to put ourselves in the coffee bar and wait for him. And so we spent a very tense half hour or so in there until he emerged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what happened after he came out?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I immediately went up to him and showed him the piece of paper and said that I had the necessary permission. And I asked him whether he would give me the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What did you do with the permission, the paper that you had been given?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I showed it to him, and I'm afraid that my memory is a blank. I don't know whether he retained it or whether he gave it back. He certainly looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did he say or do after he examined the paper that you had obtained from the Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: He told us to follow him, and he climbed into a vehicle with two bodyguards and started driving off up the road, and we followed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And these bodyguards, could you describe their appearance?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: They were not wearing a uniform, as such; in other words, there wasn't any insignia or anything like that. They were both armed with Klashnikovs. From memory, one, if not both, seemed to be dressed in sort of a dark track suit of some description.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you determine where they appeared to be from?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No. I was curious about that. I looked at one of them, and he looked to me to be, you know, possibly Kurdish. They clearly weren't Bosnian, but neither were they -- neither did they appear to be Arab. They -- they seemed very capable, very sort of confident, but I wasn't able to determine where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mentioned then you went about a half a mile to a field?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived at the field?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: We stopped behind their vehicle, and Mr. Aziz got out and said that he would conduct the interview on some rocks that were in the middle of the field. And I was immediately struck by the choice of setting, as it was almost the same setting as the -- as that chosen by one of Afghanistan's warlords, Hekmatiar, when I interviewed him months earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What seemed to be so common between those two incidents?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It was kind of a bucolic scene. It was a stream and trees and meadows. It was almost sort of a degree of tranquility. I assumed it probably was because their prophet had given sermons or something similar in similar surroundings, so I wasn't sure. I just was struck by the similarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So where was your photographer at this time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: With me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And was the interpreter still with you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And where did she sit at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I wanted to put Mr. Aziz totally at his ease, and so -- and I knew that there were issues over women, and so I asked him where he would like the photographer to sit -- sorry. I asked him where he would like the interpreter to sit, and he gestured to some rocks about 50 yards away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So you sat to take this interview with him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And where were you sitting in relation to Mr. Aziz?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Well, I suppose about four or five feet away on the rocks, facing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how did you go about memorialising this interview?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I took a shorthand note, but I also taped. I pulled out my small tape-recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And where was the tape-recorder sitting in relation to the two of you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: On the rocks between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could I have the witness shown Exhibit P01010, which I'll also explain is Exhibit P02953. And for the benefit of the Court and for the Defence, P02953 is the translation of P01010.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hogg, what do you see on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I see, on the right-hand side, the English language transcript of my interview; and, on the left-hand side, the Bosnian transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And, so, for the transcript on the right, if I could have page 2 shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hogg, have you had occasion to see this transcript today?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And were you able to confirm that this is a true and accurate transcript of the tape --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: -- of the interview you took with Mr. Aziz?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I was, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to page 2, which also bears the ERN 0081-8540. There's some handwritten notations on that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recognise those?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what are those notations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: They are notations I made when I was -- gave evidence in a previous trial here and were shown the transcript then, and determined that it contained a couple of transcription errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So this is a true and accurate copy of the document you were shown before and made markings on?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just find out, while we're on the markings, what does the bracket around "Paroba" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is, to my knowledge, no such place as Paroba. I couldn't remember what I had said. I said something like from Visoko around to, I think, it was Carola, not "Paroba." Paroba doesn't exist, but I couldn't remember what the correct name was that should replace it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hogg.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Also today, Mr. Hogg, you had a chance to hear an audiotape; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And were you able to determine that that was a true and accurate recording of the interview that you had been given?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Absolutely, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I guess I'll ask, then, on what media -- or on what medium was the interview recorded?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: A small pocket tape-recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what did you do with that tape-recorder, the tape, the cassette itself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I retained that tape, as I considered it had historic value, if nothing else. Unfortunately, the first minute or so sometime afterwards was erased, but the substance of the interview still remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: At any time, did you hand that tape over to the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I'd like for that tape to be played. For the record, that is Exhibit 02961. And for the Court's benefit, and for the benefit of Defence as well, we have synchronised the transcript, which Mr. Hogg has authenticated as his, to track along with the audio portion. So, at this time, I would like the tape to be played. And also one more thing, Your Honour. The first 30 seconds or so are a little bit garbled, and the recorded portion ends at about 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, would this be a convenient point?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was about to suggest that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Shall we come back at quarter past 4.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hogg, we've heard the audiotape.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you confirm that that is a true and accurate recording of the tape you took?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The interview with Abdel Aziz?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecutor would like to tender into evidence that audiotape, which is right now marked P02961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any objections, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The audiotape is then admitted into evidence, and May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do we apply a letter to the Prosecution exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was instructed and advised by the legal staff that we're going to adopt a continuous numbering, without prefixing it with either a Prosecution or Defence or a Chamber letter, so we would just number it as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Wood, sorry, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: That's okay, Your Honour. I'll just catch up right now with the other two that I have not yet tendered, and then I will continue very briefly. For the record, the Prosecution does tender Exhibit P01010, which is the English transcript that has been marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I guess you don't have any objection, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then that's Exhibit 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And as I understand it, Your Honour, the B/C/S translation of that transcript is attached to that exhibit. I don't know if the Registrar would like to give that another number. It's been marked right now P02953.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see the Registrar is shaking his head to indicate that he does not wish to do so, so I guess it will be 52A and B.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And, finally, the Prosecution tenders P06157, which is the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it P06157 or P16507.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: P06157. Let me make sure that's accurate. P06157.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't think that's how it was -- it appeared on the transcript when it was shown on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: To the extent that I misspoke when I said the name earlier, Your Honour, I can confirm that it is P06157; and to the extent that the transcript is wrong in that regard, I would ask that it be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. So be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Registrar wants to know whether you're tendering the entire booklet or just the one photograph. We are aware of only one photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It's just the one photograph that was shown to the witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It will be the one photograph. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, again, I assume, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P01012.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, can you describe what you see on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I see a copy of the "Sunday Times" story which I wrote, which appeared at the end of August in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, did you have a chance to look at that earlier today?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And can you confirm that that's a true and accurate record of the story that appeared in "The Sunday Times" that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And can you identify the person in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's Abdel Aziz.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And can you tell us when that photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: During -- well, as the interview was being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders P01012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May Exhibit P01012, please, be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Next, I'd like to show the witness two video segments. These are from P06001.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, can you see that video in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you identify the person holding the megaphone?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That would appear to be Abdel Aziz, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if I could have clip 2 shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, do you see the video in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And can you identify the person?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's Abdel Aziz, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: For the record, the person who's holding the megaphone. Okay. The State -- I'm sorry, the Prosecution tenders Exhibit P06001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, any objection?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear everybody if the video is being shown at the same time people are talking. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are very sorry, interpreters. What the question was, for the interpreters' purposes, was that the Prosecution was tendering this picture that you see on the clip into evidence as an exhibit. Do you hear that now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And that Madam Vidovic has said she had no objection to it being tendered as an exhibit. It is accordingly admitted into evidence, and may it please be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown Exhibit P01348.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you describe what you see on the screen in front of you, Mr. Hogg?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I see a story -- the content of a story that I wrote in the middle of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at that earlier today?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And can you confirm that that is a story that fell under your name that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders Exhibit P01348.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any objection, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Exhibit P01348 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Finally, if the exhibit -- I'm sorry. If the witness could be shown Exhibit P01682 [Realtime transcript read in error "P01632"].

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, can you describe what you see on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I see the content of the story that I wrote in January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to look at this earlier today?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I have, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And were you able to confirm that this is the story that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I can confirm that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders P01682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's P01682, not 32?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: 82, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any objection, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit P01682 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask, where was this published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In "The Sunday Times."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution has nothing further for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Wood. Madam Vidovic, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on behalf of the Defence team of General Delic, the cross-examination shall be conducted by my colleague, Nicholas Robson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Hogg. My name is Nicholas Robson, and I'll be asking you some questions on behalf of the Defence this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hogg, previously you were a journalist with "The Sunday Times." That's --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- a famous British newspaper, and I think that was from about 1980?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I started working on a part-time basis in 1980, I became a member of the staff in 1984, and I left the paper ten years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in 1991, you took over as the Middle East correspondent of that paper?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, as part of that role, you travelled to many countries. You've mentioned some of them today.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Afghanistan, Algeria, Kurdistan, Israel. You've mentioned that you encountered the Mujahedin in two of those countries: Afghanistan and Algeria. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I didn't encounter the Mujahedin in Algeria. I -- in covering the beginnings of the civil war there, I was told by numerous sources that the instigators for much of the conflict were people who had come back from the Afghan conflict. But I didn't come face to face with any Mujahedin in Algeria.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I did in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, then, that you are familiar with the concept of the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In other words, foreign fighters or "holy warriors" travelling to another country to conduct Jihad?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, am I right in saying, in Afghanistan, you spent time with the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: What I would do is distinguish between the Afghan Mujahedin, who I did indeed spend time with, I would distinguish them between the Arab Mujahedin, who formed a faction there. And as I mentioned earlier, I had, what I would term, the misfortune to come across them in the fall of a city called Gardez, and they were very hostile to my presence there. And had it not been for the fact that I was with Afghan Mujahedin, I suspect that I wouldn't be sitting here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In respect of the Afghan Mujahedin that you met, am I correct in understanding that you met one of Afghanistan's warlords, Hehmatiar?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Hehmatiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Hehmatiar?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Hehmatiar, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And I think it is right to say that on once occasion whilst you were in Afghanistan, you even disguised yourself as a Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's how I got into Afghanistan, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you do that in order to collect more information about them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No. I had -- I tried -- I had been sent to Afghanistan in 1989, when the Soviets withdrew. And I had been, on arrival, arrested at the airport and held overnight and deported and on the first plane out. So when several years later I had to go back to Afghanistan, I determined not to go by air. I thought my chances of reaching Kabul would be better by going over land.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I see. It's right to say you must have developed a good level of knowledge about the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel and the witness kindly pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You knew how they functioned?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that would be fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you gained an idea of how the Arab Mujahedin were financed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I gained the strong impression that they didn't want very much in the way of equipment in Afghanistan. Their brand-new Walkie-Talkies were rather different to what I had seen the Afghan fighters use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You gained the impression that the Arab Mujahedin were well equipped?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you gained an insight about their ideas and goals; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I didn't gain it from them. I gained it from -- from other people there. It was quite clear they were there fighting Jihad. It was quite clear that they had a considerable reputation for bravery. It was also quite clear to me that they seemed to be a law unto themselves, to the extent that I did ask Afghan Mujahedin what they would do with them after a government had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did they give you an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes. The answer I was given was that they would have to obey the laws of the country; otherwise, they would be told to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So you said they were there fighting Jihad. Would you agree that their goal was to conduct holy war?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree that not all the Mujahedin had the same approach to religion, so there would be differences amongst them; some would be Wuhabi, you would have Salifi, Shiite; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would presume that's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is it right that those religion differences, as far as you can tell us, were one of the reasons why there were divisions amongst the Mujahedin in Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer that with any degree of assurance. I -- you know, the Arabs that I saw there were, I would have thought, probably Sunni, and the Afghan Mujahedin were Sunni as well, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. If I may interrupt, Mr. Wood is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, Your Honour, it might be helpful to the Trial Chamber to get some clarification about, on this line of questioning, is Mr. Hogg speaking of Afghan Mujahedin or is he speaking of the Mujahedin in Bosnia. I'm following the transcript, and I think that might not be that clear. And so on those grounds, I do objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And while you clarify that, if it is the Afghan Mujahedin, is it the Afghan Mujahedin and not the Arab Mujahedin that he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, perhaps you could help us with that. I'm just looking at the transcript, and I think that your last answer was perhaps dealing with that very point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is it correct you were saying that the Afghan Mujahedin were Sunni?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. And the Arab Mujahedin in Afghanistan, I would assume to have been Sunni as well. There may have been divisions, but I wasn't aware of those divisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, does that clarify the point sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It does also to me. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, I'd like to show you our first exhibit, if I may. It's D15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOGG
utterances.text: If we can perhaps get that up on the screen, and the relevant page of that document is the third page of that document. Please, if we could have a close-up on the first paragraph just straight under: "Jihad comes to Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could read that passage to you, Mr. Hogg, it says: "The Charter of Islamic Struggle. We, as Muslims, have been given the task to realise the supremacy of the law of God on earth and of not allowing that any group on earth govern without the law of God. We fight whoever refuses that and refuses obedience to God. "The fight is imposed on us to remove the apostate ruler from the land of Islam, to fight those who support them and their laws, to impose the caliphate, to revenge Palestine, Spain, the Balkans, the Islamic Republics in Russia, and to free the Muslim prisoners. Our enemies are Christians, Jews, apostates, those who adore the cow and fire, our secular rulers that replace the laws of Islam, and hypocrites. "Jihad has been introduced to spread God's religion and to destroy any ruler that is not subject to the adoration of God. Fighting the infidels has the purpose of exalting the revelation God." That is a document found by the Italian police at the Islamic Cultural Institute, ICI, in Milan. And, perhaps, before I ask my quest, I should also point out that this exhibit is an excerpt from the book "Al-Qaeda's Jihad in Europe: The Afghan Bosnia Network." That's a book by the Prosecution's expert witness, Evan Coleman. My question, Mr. Hogg, is: Would you agree that the principles espoused in that document found in Milan reflect the principles of the Mujahedin that you met in Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I think undoubtedly, yeah, reflect the principles of the Arab Mujahedin that I met in Afghanistan. The Afghan Mujahedin, you know, deeply religious though they were, I couldn't say that they would necessarily subscribe to that kind of totalitarian vision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you for making that distinction. Your Honour, could I please tender that document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Does Defence speak of the entire book or just this excerpt?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's just this excerpt, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just the excerpt, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Wood. Exhibit D15 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number 58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Turning to your interview with Mr. Aziz, he explained to you that the Mujahedin fighters were coming to Bosnia to conduct Jihad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: He told you about some of the countries that the fighters had come from. You mentioned England and Germany?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Mmm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And Abdel Aziz told you that he himself had carried out Jihad in Afghanistan, the Philippines, Kashmir, and Africa; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, from what you observed in Bosnia, would you agree with me that the Mujahedin that came from Afghanistan and other places brought those ideas that we just discussed a moment ago with them to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I think, yes, I'd say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: During your interview with Abdel Aziz, it's right that he explained to you certain rules of behaviour of the Mujahedin, such as Shaddah and Dawa; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: As to Shaddah, you said that this means being killed in battle for Islam?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Concerning Dawa, he explained to you that it was the duty of the Mujahedin to give the Bosnian people, to use his words, what is the correct Islam?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: He also discussed finances, and he explained to you that the Mujahedin received financial support from many Islamic countries; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It was a little unclear, but as I understood it, he also indicated that they were receiving financial support from individuals as well as governments. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would have to re-examine the transcript. I wouldn't argue that at all. I don't recollect him really saying that they were receiving help from governments. My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My recollection is that he actually said they don't receive from governments; they only receive from individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
