utterances.text: If I can refer again to the last exhibit just entered, Exhibit 58, this time we were -- I beg your pardon. What I should say, if I could refer to Defence document D15, this is another excerpt from the Evan Kohlmann book. It's at page 4 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, we're interested in the bottom quarter of that page, if we could perhaps get a close-up of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel kindly be asked to slow down when reading for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, if I can read to you a passage from that final paragraph. It states, just four lines down from the -- the start beginning a bit after "Witnessing." It says: "Abu Abdel Aziz had no allusions about his mission in Bosnia. Though he spent part of his time encouraging Dawa, Islamic missionary work, he cautioned, 'We are not here to bring supplies like food and medicine. There are lots of organisations that can do that. We bring men.' Upon his arrival, the Mujahedin leadership in Bosnia and Afghanistan designated Sheikh Abu Abdel Aziz as the first emir, or commander-in-chief, of the Bosnian Arab Afghans. The new emir quickly established his first headquarters at the Mehurici training camp near the central Bosnian town of Travnik." Now, Mr. Hogg, do you agree from that excerpt that you can conclude that the Mujahedin leadership in Afghanistan, as well as Bosnia, took the decision to designate Aziz as their commander-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah, I accept that's what it says on the page. I have no way of knowing how true that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you confirm for us, from your experiences, that it was usual practice, if you like, for the Mujahedin leadership to appoint the commander; is that something you've come across?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm that, I'm afraid. I just have no way of knowing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, could I tender that document, that page, into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, based on what the witness has said, he says he can't accept -- he can accept that that's what's written on the page, but he can't confirm the truth of that. And for that reason, the Prosecution does object to the admission of this into evidence. I don't believe it's properly authenticated at this point or the proper context has been given it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps, if I could ask a further question. Well, first of all, Your Honour, just to point out that the book was written by the Prosecution's expert, Evan Kohlmann. And the second point I would make, Your Honour, is the that Defence will be adducing evidence in due course that pertains to this matter to make the connection; and if necessary, I can ask the witness a further question that may perhaps clarify the probity of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you ask the witness the question, Mr. Robson, if I may just ask, you're saying that Mr. Kohlmann is a Prosecution expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you're saying the excerpt comes from his book?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to be calling Mr. Kohlmann as a witness yourself, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he's a Prosecution witness, and it remains to be seen whether he'll be called by the Prosecution, but he's certainly a witness that's interesting to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true. You said you're going to call another witness who can testify to the probity of the document. Is that Mr. Kohlmann or is it somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, What we would seek to do is call furthers witnesses that discuss the matters mentioned in excerpts that I have just read out. So if perhaps the purpose of that evidence is not clear to you at the moment, it will do so in due course, we hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would it be inconvenient to the Defence if I suggested that maybe you wait for Mr. Kohlmann to come; and when you do cross-examine him, you tender that exhibit through him? He's the author?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Indeed he is, he is. Your Honour, that's something that certainly the Defence could do. Perhaps, if I could ask a further question, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's of Mr. Hogg.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What I would just ask Mr. Hogg is that: In the excerpt that I read out, it referred to Sheikh Abu Abdel Aziz as being the first emir, and he established his first headquarters in Mehurici. Can you confirm, Mr. Hogg, that the person that you spoke to was indeed Abu Abdel Aziz, and you interviewed him very close to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know what that has to do with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would be satisfied for perhaps it to be marked for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we can deal with it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What is this? This is page 4 of Exhibit 58. It will be marked for identification, and may it please be given a number for identification?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked for identification, MFI, as number 59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, if we could turn to the article that you wrote and was published on the 30th of August, 1992, in "The Sunday Times." It's Prosecution Exhibit 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if I can refer the Court's attention to the third column, it's the paragraph -- it's about the third paragraph down -- I beg your pardon. If we could move up from that section. We have it there. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, I'd like to refer your attention to the paragraph that begins: "The leader of the Mujahedin." And if I could read that section to you, it states as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- "The leader of the Mujahedin in Bosnia, Abu Abdel Aziz, said his men had no intention of interfering in Bosnia's internal politics." Now, Mr. Hogg, from what you knew about the Mujahedin, is it not correct that it would be almost impossible for them to conduct holy war and remain clear of local politics? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would agree with that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's true to say that wherever the Mujahedin fought, their aim was to create an Islamic state?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would agree with that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, in preparing this article, you spoke to various people; and in your evidence earlier today, you told us about the occasion when you spoke to some men, military people, outside of the retirement home in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It was actually inside the retirement home. We were sitting in there, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's right, isn't it, that when you spoke to them, to those men, you recorded details in a notebook that you had with you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could refer the witness to the notebook, it's Defence document D14, and the page we're interested in is page 27.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, okay. Although it's 27 for the purposes of the document, it's actually page 28 of the notebook that we're interested in, and it's that very last piece of text: "We are fighting ..."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I can just read out that quotation, one of them told you: "We are fighting for our lives and the lives of our children. What Islamic republic." [Realtime transcript read in error "?"] Is it correct, Mr. Hogg, that that was said to you in response to a question you put to the men?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree it's clear from their words that the main concern of these men was simple survival and protection. They were not interested in fighting to create an Islamic state, were they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would agree with that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Robson --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- In the transcript, the last word appears with a question mark, "What Islamic republic?" I don't see the question a question mark in the notebook; and, indeed, I wonder, what does that last three words really mean? Could you clarify, Mr. Hogg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I would undoubtedly have tried to gauge from those soldiers that I was interviewing what their view was of the claim that Izetbegovic wanted to establish an Islamic republic in Bosnia. That was a claim that was made by the Serb aggressors, and it was, you know, something that I would undoubtedly have asked, particularly because of their relationship with the Mujahedin, who I would have been under no doubt were, in truth, hopeful of advancing the cause of an Islamic republic. I would have asked these soldiers, you know, "What are your views?" Is there -- are they here fighting for an Islamic republic or what? And if you look at the paragraph above, it says they were fighting for Izetbegovic's vision of a civilian government in Bosnia. I'm afraid it's 15 years and I can't remember, with absolute precision, the questions that I asked, but I know that I would have asked them. You've got the Mujahedin here. Is this part of an attempt to establish an Islamic republic, and that would have been the reply, "What Islamic republic. We're fighting for our lives."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So did you have a distinction between different kinds of Islamic republics in mind? And if so, just an Islamic republic, full stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Not a question of whether it would be Sunni or Shiite or any other kind of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just an Islamic republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you carry on, Mr. Robson, let me just clear up a little work in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: These men you were interviewing were Bosniak soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you did write an article from this interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This interview was when I was trying to find the Mujahedin. When I found Abdel Aziz, the article that I wrote was based purely on what he had told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you never wrote an article --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- residing from these notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, from these notes, there was maybe one paragraph that appeared in the final article, which was to do with these men are, you know, the bravest of the brave. They walk where others crawl. I think that comment came from talking to these Bosnian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if you look at that paragraph, would that paragraph not jog your memory as to the context within which this little statement was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I mean, I'm pretty clear about the context. It's just the precise wording that I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it wouldn't jog your memory about the precise wording, either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid it wouldn't, not after this passage of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can't take it any further. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So it's clear, then, Mr. Hogg, that Abdel Aziz and his Mujahedin would have had very different goals to those young men that you spoke to at the retirement home?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I think that that is -- that is absolutely correct to say. When I interviewed Abdel Aziz and he gave off this image of being a sort of perfectly reasonable, helpful human being, I didn't buy into that, necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hogg, I'd like to refer you to a different part of your notebook. This is page 19, page 19 of the document as well. And I should say that this part of your notebook concerns the different units that you encountered in the field.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, perhaps, if we could have as much as possible of page 19 on the screen, and we're interested in about halfway down that page. I should say at the very top of the document we can see it's marked pages 19 and 20, so it's page 19. If we can perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hogg, about halfway down, in the middle of the screen, we can see there -- it's very difficult to see what you're writing, particularly, but we can make out some words?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we can make out the words: "HVO, Bosnian forces, TO, and HOS"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Mmm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Underneath that, we can see: "Bosnian Army." And if we look just at the bottom of the page there, just above the third line from bottom, we can see the words: "Muslim Defence Forces"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Similarly, if we go over onto page 20, about halfway down that page, if we can move over to the following page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just below the halfway stage, again, a little hard to see, but we can make out there the words -- it says: "200 MOS soldiers," M-O-S soldiers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hogg, at the time that you made these notes, would you agree that you had very little or no knowledge about the structure of the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I had the barest knowledge about the structure of the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it follows from that that you must have had little or no understanding about the system of control in the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would say that's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: However, from your observations and who you spoke to, you were -- although you knew little or nothing about the army's structure, you did note the presence of different military units in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And there, in the notebook, we can note where you've identified those different units?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: When you interviewed Abdel Aziz, he didn't tell you very much about the different units in Central Bosnia, did he?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: But do you recall, he did mention the name of a unit, Muslim Forces, and the Mujahedin's ties with them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not -- wouldn't necessarily think he was referring to a specific unit by that. My understanding at the time, as it is now, is that that was a shorthand way of describing the Bosnian armed force forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I go any further, perhaps I should tender the notebook as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The entire notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The entire notebook, I would ask, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The entire notebook will be -- is admitted into evidence as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hogg, I'd like to show you two further documents. The first document is Defence document D21. It's another interview with Abu Abdel Aziz which he gave in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I should say that it's pages 2 and 3 of that document that we're interested in. Perhaps before I read out the text, would it be possible just to go back to the front page so that I can confirm to the Court indeed that this is an article that Abdel Aziz gave. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So we can see it was an article that appeared in the "Ad-Dawah" magazine in Pakistan, January 1993, headed: "The Jihad in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Written by the witness, Mr. Hogg?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was not by Mr. Hogg, but it was -- the interviewee was the same person that Mr. Hogg interviewed, Abdel Aziz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, perhaps, if we could turn to page 2 that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Who was the author of the article?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: A very good question. Your Honour, I don't believe the author is named in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Where was it published?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It was published in Pakistan, and the magazine was "Ad-Dawah," and it was in January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, perhaps, if we can focus on the second half of this document, the part beginning: "In view of the situation ..." If I could read that out to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What it says is: "In view of the situation, we wondered whether it was permissible to make Jihad with these people; these people, who drank alcohol and committed adultery, even to the extent that they drink at the war front. There were also females in the military forces with a lot of promiscuity going on. However, Alhamd-u-lillah, when we prayed to Allah to guide us on whether we should make Jihad and fight, we found a group which consisted of Muslims. "They were mainly Imams, many from Saudi Arabia, Khaleej, and students from various universities around the world. They had begun working under the banner of 'Islamic Muslim Forces.' They also said that to fight alongside with the official military forces against the Kuffar was not fighting in the way of Allah. Alhamd-u-lillah, this group had prepared more than nine military units fighting at different locations and instituted some requirements for anyone who wanted to join them. This included praying five times daily, no alcohol consumption, no fornication or adultery, and no use of foul language. "These were the basic requirements, which the Bosnian Muslims considered very tough. These were the people who started the Jihad, and whenever we come across any Arab brothers, we would tell them to go to their country and inform their community that a Jihad had started in Bosnia to inform them that their is a group called Muslim Forces that has the right, "akida" [phoen]; and whoever wants to come, let him come."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, that last part is obviously on the next page. Perhaps if we can take a look at the next page to confirm that. Thank you. Before I pose any question, I'd like to put another document to Mr. Hogg, and this is -- or perhaps rather than using a document, it may be possible to use the tape-recording that the Prosecution played earlier, Exhibit 51. I don't know if that's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Everything is always possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I noted the timing of the particular section that I was interested in, and it's three minutes 40, so perhaps if we could play that part again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I guess it's going to be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can pause it there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So my question, Mr. Hogg: In both the article -- the interview, I should say, given by Abdel Aziz in Pakistan in January 1993, and also during the interview which he gave with you in August 1992, he made it clear that the Mujahedin in Bosnia were related to the Muslim forces, didn't he? And perhaps it's right to say, isn't it, at no point, during that interview that was played to the Court today, did he actually mention the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's correct, not during the tape transcript, but his insistent that we got the permission from the Bosnian Army --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: There was a reference to the Bosnian Army at that point.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. May I just ask a question. When he asked you again for permission to interview him, who did he refer you to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the Bosnian Army was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The interview, Your Honour, was the point I was trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, in the article that appeared in Pakistan that I read out, concerning the Imams and students that he met, Abdel Aziz explained: "They also said that to fight alongside with the official military forces against the Khaffar was not fighting in the way of Allah." Would you accept that Aziz is saying that those Imams told the Mujahedin that they should not fight alongside the official military forces in Bosnia; in other words, the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would accept that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, could I tender those exhibits into evidence? I should say that the source of the first document, the article, it's come from the Prosecution and it's a document that was referred to in the expert witness report of Evan Kohlmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before I tend to Mr. Wood, can I just understand that this article, that was written in January of '93 in Afghanistan, is it talking about the Bosnian war?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Indeed, yes, Your Honour. It's an article that was written in January 1993. It appeared in a Pakistani magazine. It was -- the interviewee was Abu Abdel Aziz, and it was talking about the Bosnian war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You're tendering two exhibits. I've got here Exhibit D21. Is that what you want to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clarify, the audiotape that we've just listened to is already in evidence, so it's the one exhibit. It's the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Exhibit D21 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, also in connection with the Abdel Aziz that I've just read out, perhaps at this stage I could ask that the video that the Prosecution played earlier be played once again concerning the formation of the 7th Muslim Brigade. It's Exhibit 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Did the Defence have any particular segment or portion of that tape in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, no. If we could just play a small excerpt, that would be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It could be from the beginning, just the same as it was, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: There's no need to go further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, in this video, we can see, with the man identified as Abdel Aziz, is a religion man. That's the Imam of Travnik, Efendi Nusret Avdibegovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree that their presence together would correspond with the part of the interview given by Abdel Aziz, where he said that found the found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we stop, please. We have the French coming through the English channel. Can we have some help?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. That was a mistake of the French interpreters. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you put the question again, and let's get the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So it's in connection with the article that appeared in the Pakistani "Ad-Dawah" magazine. We can see here together Abdel Aziz with a religion man, the Efendi, the Imam of Travnik. Would you agree their presence together corresponded with that part of their interview given by Mr. Aziz, where he said that they found a group consisting mainly imams?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I would say it corresponds. Whether that's accurate or not, I just don't know, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, we can leave that video. We're going to turn to the article dated 27th of June, 1993, which is Prosecution Exhibit 56. Perhaps if we can have that document up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if we can -- if we can focus on the second paragraph in the top half of that document, it's the paragraph beginning: "More than 200 Mujahedin ..." If I can quote that, it states: "More than 200 Mujahedin, who have been fighting in Bosnia for the past year, now operate as lawless gangs which the Bosnian Command is powerless to control." First of all, Mr. Hogg, you've confirmed today that you wrote that article?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I have, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And as an experienced career journalist, this was your informed conclusion, wasn't it, that those Mujahedin operated as lawless gangs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: By that time, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And at that stage, the Bosnian Command was powerless to control them as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Well, clearly the colonel that I met in the street in Zenica, whose comments formed the basis for this, considered that they were beyond the Bosnian Army control. I wouldn't have any reason to doubt that, although one aspect that has always confused me is the relationship between 7th Brigade and other Bosnian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can refer to the third paragraph, following on from what you just told us, it's right that you also referred to the Mujahedin as "freelance fighters"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Mmm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And by that do I take it to mean that they operated freely, without having to obey anybody?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: As far as my information was, that was pretty much the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then the final part from this particular article, it's down towards the bottom of the page. It sits within the paragraph: "Since we he made the promise, that promise last year ..." There's one sentence I would like to read out to you. It states: "When a truck carrying Islamic soldiers collided with a UN vehicle, the Mujahedin threatened to kill the Muslim judge who heard the case against them." Again, would you agree, Mr. Hogg, that that's a further indication that the Mujahedin had no respect for the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hogg, I'd like to turn the Court's attention to the document that you received prior to interviewing Abdel Aziz. You've explained to the Court that Abdel Aziz told you that you needed permission from the military. At that point, you returned to Travnik; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that that was the only official paper that you received from the authorities during your travels in the region on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: On that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: At that time.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It was the only bit of paper that I got that satisfied Abdel Aziz, but I'm pretty sure that I would have had other -- other paperwork to have been able to move around the region freely. But certainly that's the only piece of paper that had any relevance as far as he was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've told us how the translator obtained that document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: She was inside the command -- or the building, let's say, for ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And she came out; and, at some stage, you saw that document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you don't speak the local language, Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: However, it looked official and it had a stamp on it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: My memory of precisely what it contained is hazy, but I have no doubt that it would have had a stamp on it to testify to its validity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, based on the countries that you had visited as a journalist, is it fair to say that you travelled in war zones before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that during a wartime situation, when there were journalists in the field, a risk might arise that a journalist could publish a story and reveal sensitive information about military targets or personnel in a certain area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's certainly not unusual to require journalists to have special permission to move into combat areas, is it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: It is absolutely routine and has been for a very long time. As I understand it, in the Spanish Civil War, one of the complaints was the bits of paper you needed to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I could refer the Court's attention to Defence document D16, this is a document that there should be both B/C/S and English versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hogg, we can see this is a document of the operative group Bosanska Krajina, based in Travnik, and it's dated 9th of June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we can see from this document that this is an approval which allows for entry into specified war zones by a number of named journalists?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what the document states is that the subordinate units and individuals will provide the necessary assistance to the above-mentioned persons?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's possible, is it not, Mr. Hogg, that the document you received, or shall I say your interpreter received, was just like this one, a generalised document granting access to enter a war zone, stating officially that you were a journalist rather than being addressed to a particular individual; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Frankly, not, no. My understanding was that the piece of paper that I was given was specifically the granting of permission to interview Abdel Aziz. I think that I would probably have already had other paperwork given to me to be able to work in that area. The other thing to bear in mind is that this document was issued almost a year after the interview that I conducted, by which time, given the very large number of journalists working in Central Bosnia, the whole press operation had become much more sophisticated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, let's just consider what you've said. You've told us that your understanding was that it was specific information to speak with Abdel Aziz?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Specific permission, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Permission?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: But earlier on, during your testimony, as I understand it, you've explained to the Court that at no time were those words used; all the words that you used were you needed the necessary permission. That's my understanding of your evidence earlier on during evidence-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I needed the necessary permission for him to agree to talk to me. I had to present him with something which said that the Bosnian Army allowed me to interview Abdel Aziz. That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, you've told us you looked at this document, you said it looked official, there was a stamp on it. You haven't mentioned, but there was no name of Abdel Aziz on there, was there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I've said two or three times now that I can't remember precisely what was on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Because if the document was written in Bosnian, the name would remain the same, wouldn't it? You would still --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Of course, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, surely, that would be something significant that would perhaps stick in your mind?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Not really. It was -- it was at night. Yeah, we were elated we had got the necessary permission to go and interview Abdel Aziz. I just have no recollection of what appeared on that piece of paper at all, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just bear with me for one moment, please. Thank you, Mr. Hogg. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I beg your pardon. Perhaps just before I sit down, I believe, yes, I would like to tender that document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's D16?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That is D16, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. D16 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before you let the witness go, Mr. Robson, I'd like to put a question to the witness which you can still cross-examine on them. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And perhaps it's a legal question that you cannot answer, and if that is the case, then please do not attempt to answer it, but simply say that you can't, but my question refers to the status of the Mujahedin. And what I want to ask you is if you were ever offered any information about whether the Mujahedin troops were considered as mercenaries or considered as regular members of the ABiH. The distinction can be difficult to draw for someone who's not an expert on international humanitarian law. But in the terms of the Geneva Conventions, it does make a difference. So were you at any point offered any evidence or could you form any opinion as to whether the Mujahedin were to be classified as mercenaries or as regular members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: What I would say is that in the early days of the conflict, I believe that the relationship did exist. There were several instances involving acquaintances of mine coming across the Mujahedin and the Mujahedin being in the company of members of the Bosnian military. But by the time I came to write the story in June 1993, my impression is that a degree of radicalisation had taken place, that new fighters had come into the country, and at that stage -- by that stage I think that it would correct probably to look at them as effectively as mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't wish to pose any questions following that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. Mr. Wood, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution has nothing further at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions, Judge? Any questions for you, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one or two questions to clarify in my own mind, Mr. Hogg. At page 16 of the transcript today, lines 19 to 23, if somebody can help you to get there, you made reference to the fact that the Serb and Croat military personnel were on the same side. I don't know whether you can remember that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would need to see the page of the transcript. I was referring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's I was asking if somebody could help you to get there. Can somebody help you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's there on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Look at the screen there.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. What I said was that the Bosnians and the Croats were on the same side against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Bosnians and the Croats --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Were on the same side against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I obviously had miswritten. Thank you very much for that clarification. You individually, as a human being just in that area, were you able to distinguish, by looking or even by talking, between Bosnians and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, at page 23, lines 2 to 5, you said that two of some dozen military men that you met wore a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: This is when I first came across the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. No, two of them wore local military uniform. In other words, they were identifiable as members of the Bosnian military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How did you identify them as members of the Bosnian military?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I can only assume it was the uniforms that they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you see any insignia on them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: That is -- that's not something I could state with absolute certainty, but there was no doubt in my mind that they were Bosnian. So then I must have seen something that indicated that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. There was two?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: I would say there was two out of the group of about a dozen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to remember how the rest were dressed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW HOGG
utterances.text: Yeah. The rest were dressed in sort of a hodge-podge of different military/camouflage clothing. Some of the -- I already mentioned one of them, for instance, was wearing a dark track suit, but others would have had either camouflage jackets or camouflage trousers, or in some cases both. So there was no uniformity to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That concludes my questions. Mr. Wood, do you have any questions arising from the questions from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I might assist the Trial Chamber, Your Honour, if the witness could clarify, when he refers to Bosnians, what exactly does he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when he refers to Croats --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when he refers to Serbs --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian Serbs, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robson, any questions arising from the Bench's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Hogg, that brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming. The Trial Chamber would like to express its gratitude for you availing yourself, I'm sure you've got a very busy schedule, and taking time off to come and testify. Thank you very much. You are now excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next witness who's scheduled to testify is not ready to commence his testimony today, so we would propose that we adjourn at this point, and he will be ready to commence his testimony at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do not think that we are sitting tomorrow, not according to the court schedule. I haven't seen it. I believe my court schedule is outdated. We are sitting tomorrow at 2.15. In which court? The same courtroom. Thank you very much. And that being so, before we adjourn, I would like to just deal with a small housekeeping matter. Am I right -- I've just sort of been literally calling for breaks, and I'm not quite sure whether this accords with the requirements of the interpreters, in particular, and the taping. But previously, in a previous case, I have sat -- we have sat here for one and a quarter hours per session; that is, if we start at quarter past 2.00, we would go from quarter past 2.00 until half past 3.00, take a 30-minute break and go on like that. Does that suit everybody? Judge Harhoff tells me normally it's one and a half hours. And how long are the breaks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We were taking one and a quarter hours and 30 minutes' breaks, okay. I'm not quite sure which way you want to go. One and a half hours, 20 minutes' breaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We're certainly in the hands of the Trial Chamber. It's up to the Trial Chamber, as far as the Prosecution is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll talk about it and we'll give a final ruling when we next meet tomorrow afternoon. Mr. Registrar, do you want to say something? Okay. In that event, then the Court stands adjourned until tomorrow afternoon at quarter past 2.00 in the same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
